title: SRE: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning & Runbooks (Guidance)
author: Ari Chen
content:
Summary

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's recommended practices for SRE documentation covering SLOs and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and runbook templates. It is intended for service owners, SREs, and platform engineers who operate and evolve inference services across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Goals

- Provide a single, repeatable approach for defining and governing SLOs and error budgets.
- Standardize capacity planning inputs and runbook actions to reduce outage time and cost.
- Define incident review and postmortem expectations so reliability improvements are measurable.
- Describe essential operational tooling and dashboards required for day-to-day operations.
- Supply runbook templates with clear ownership and escalation paths.

Audience and scope

- Audience: SRE team, service owners, product managers (when SLOs affect customer experience), and on-call engineers.
- Scope: Infra and service-level SLOs for inference APIs, scheduling and serving runtime, cache layers, and admin/management endpoints. Not in scope: ML model evaluation metrics (handled by Applied ML docs).

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Definition and tiering

- SLO: a measurable objective for user-visible reliability over a rolling 30-day window unless otherwise noted.
- Service tiers:
  - Tier 1 (Critical user-facing inference APIs): Availability 99.95%, P99 latency target, error budget 0.05% over 30 days.
  - Tier 2 (Non-critical APIs, internal tooling): Availability 99.9%, P95 latency target, error budget 0.1% over 30 days.
  - Tier 3 (Background jobs, batch workflows): Availability 99.5%, throughput targets, error budget 0.5% over 30 days.

SLO component guidance (use these fields in every SLO document)

- SLO name: short, unique (eg 'inference-text-generate:availability').
- Owner: service/product owner and primary SRE.
- User-visible metric: choose 1 primary metric (eg success rate, end-to-end latency).
- Window: 30d default; 7d for highly volatile services; 90d for long-term batch workloads.
- Target and why: brief justification tied to customer impact.
- Measurement method: data source, query, aggregation, and sampling considerations.
- Error budget policy: depletion thresholds and automated actions (see below).

Measurement examples

- Availability: success_rate = successful_requests / total_requests (exclude healthchecks and scheduled maintenance).
- Latency: measure end-to-end server processing time; use client-facing percentiles (P50/P90/P99) with request size buckets.

Error budget policy and automation

- Green: remaining error budget > 50% — normal engineering cadence.
- Yellow: remaining error budget 10% - 50% — restrict low-priority releases; require SRE approval for canary expansion.
- Red: remaining error budget < 10% — freeze risky releases; require incident review for mitigation and rollback.

Automated actions (examples)

1. Alert to SRE channel when error budget drops below 50%.
2. Auto-pause scheduled non-critical batch jobs when below 25%.
3. Automatically route traffic to higher-capacity pools when predictable latency regressions detected and runbook conditions met.

2) Capacity planning

Inputs and signals

- Traffic forecasts: 90th and 99th percentile forecasts by route, obtained from usage analytics.
- Performance profiles: per-model and per-sequence-length throughput and latency curves (from benchmarking suite).
- Packing/batching efficiency: expected tokens-per-batch, KV cache hit rates.
- Safety buffer: 20% on top of expected peak for Tier 1 services unless SLA contract specifies higher.

Capacity calculation (summary formula)

- Required GPUs = ceil( (expected_peak_tokens_per_second * average_tokens_per_request) / (tokens_per_gpu_second * batching_efficiency) * (1 + safety_buffer) )

- Document assumptions explicitly in the capacity worksheet: traffic window, average sequence length, model variant used, quantization profile, and observed batch sizes.

Scaling policy and runbook tie-in

- Autoscale thresholds should be defined based on queue length and P95 latency breaches.
- Runbooks must include explicit steps to add/remove capacity and to failover to alternate model variants or regions.

Capacity review cadence

- Monthly capacity review for Tier 1 services and quarterly for Tier 2/3.
- Before major product launches, host a pre-launch capacity runbook review 2 weeks prior.

3) Reliability initiatives and improvement program

- Track reliability initiatives as short-lived projects with measurable KPIs (eg reduce P99 latency by 30% for route X, reduce instance OOMs from 4/month to 0/month).
- Use the following lifecycle: Identify -> Hypothesize -> Develop mitigation -> Canary -> Measure -> Rollout -> Close with retrospective and owner.
- Prioritize initiatives against error budget impact and customer-visible regressions.

4) Incident review standards (postmortems)

Expectations

- All Sev 2+ incidents require a written postmortem within 72 hours of incident mitigation. Sev 1 require an initial report in 24 hours and a full postmortem in 7 days.
- Postmortem should be blameless, clearly identify impact, timeline, root cause(s), contributing factors, and concrete action items with owners and due dates.

Postmortem template (required sections)

1. Title and incident ID
2. Severity, start/end times, duration
3. Summary of impact (customers, internal metrics)
4. Timeline (timestamped events)
5. Root cause and contributing factors
6. Detection and mitigation steps taken
7. Why was this not detected earlier (signals missing)
8. Remediation and prevention actions (owner + ETA)
9. Follow-ups (link to related change requests, CI runs, config changes)

Action tracking and verification

- All action items created from postmortems must be tracked in the reliability board and verified within the stated ETA. The SRE lead must mark items verified or escalate to engineering leadership.

5) Operational tooling and dashboards

Minimum dashboards per service

- Health overview: success rate, request rate, error rate, rolling window SLO status.
- Latency distribution: P50/P90/P99 by request size and model variant.
- Capacity and utilization: GPU count, CPU, mem, queue length, batch sizes.
- Error taxonomy: most common error types (model OOM, runtime OOM, network timeouts, tokenization errors).
- On-call runbook links and recent deploys.

Alerts and thresholds (guidance)

- SLO burn rate alert: trigger at burn rate > 4 for 1 hour (or equivalent to crossing the Yellow threshold).
- Latency escalation: P99 exceed target for 5m -> page SRE.
- Capacity risk: queue length > configured threshold and utilization > 85% for 10m -> page SRE.

Tooling integrations

- Logging: structured request IDs, model variant, trace IDs must be present in logs.
- Tracing: distributed traces for end-to-end latency with sampling keyed by error and high-latency requests.
- Cost telemetry: token-level cost estimates surfaced on the dashboard for capacity decisions.

6) Runbooks (templates and examples)

Runbook naming conventions

- Use short names: service-action-target (eg inference-api-high-latency, inference-model-oom). Include major owners in metadata.

Runbook: inference-api-high-latency (summary)

- Detection: P99 > target for 5 minutes OR SLO burn rate alert.
- Immediate steps (0-15 minutes):
  1. Announce in #sre-incidents with summary and incident channel.
  2. Identify recent deploys (last 30m). If deploy exists, begin rollback plan.
  3. Check queue length, batch sizes, and GPU utilization.
  4. If GPU utilization > 90% and queue growing, scale up pool or shift traffic to Dedicated failover pool.
- Mitigation (15-60 minutes):
  1. Revert suspect deploy if canary or recent release correlates with regression.
  2. Temporarily disable non-essential background jobs.
  3. Route heavy routes to lower-cost high-throughput model variant if quality acceptable.
- Post-incident: open postmortem and create action items.

Runbook: inference-model-oom

- Detection: Out-of-memory errors with model worker restarts or eviction events.
- Immediate steps:
  1. Remove problematic model traffic (reroute) or reduce concurrency for that model.
  2. Increase instance memory or switch to a quantized variant if tested.
  3. Collect logs: container OOM messages, kernel OOM killer entries, runtime traces.
- Mitigation and verification: ensure model worker stability for 30m before returning to normal traffic.

Runbook: control-plane-degraded

- Detection: control plane API error rate increase or inability to schedule new jobs.
- Immediate steps:
  1. Check leader election status, DB connectivity, and KMS availability.
  2. If DB is slow, enable read-only fallbacks and scale DB read replicas.
  3. Alert product and sales if customer impact expected.

7) Ownership, review cadence, and docs lifecycle

- Document owner: every SLO/runbook must list a primary owner (SRE) and secondary owner (service).
- Review cadence: SLOs reviewed quarterly; runbooks reviewed semi-annually or after any major incident.
- Documentation standards: follow confluence documentation guidelines. Include measurement queries, dashboard links, and runbook test procedures.

8) Runbook testing and gamedays

- Runbook verification: require an on-call runbook drill quarterly for Tier 1 services. Drills should validate detection, playbook steps, and escalation.
- Gamedays: simulate capacity failures, region failovers, and model OOM scenarios annually. Capture lessons learned as reliability initiatives.

Appendix: Example measurement queries and config snippets

- Example success rate (PromQL):
  sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="inference-api",status!~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="inference-api"}[5m]))

- Example SLO alert (pseudo):
  - name: SLO Burn Rate
    expr: burn_rate_over_1h > 4 and slo_remaining < 0.5
    for: 5m
    severity: warn

- Capacity worksheet columns (CSV friendly): service, route, model_variant, avg_seq_len, tokens_per_req, reqs_per_sec_99p, tokens_per_gpu_sec, batching_efficiency, safety_buffer, required_gpus, owner
